creators.name: Kallaway
creators.desc: Explains the brain science of attention: prediction, loops, hooks, and the words that hold people.

creators.name: Caleb Ralston
creators.desc: Turns stories into a world people want to live in: belief, credibility, names, characters, lore.

creators.name: Sam Gaudet
creators.desc: Ships it fast with a phone: context plus conflict, one idea per video, delivery, and reps.

creators.name: Aayush Swamy
creators.desc: Every Reel is a numbered, proof-heavy structure with a clear job: get found, build trust, or sell.

creators.name: Adley Kinsman
creators.desc: Founder of Viralish. Treats a video as a testable unit: engineer the hook for retention, design the comment section before filming, then split test everything.

creators.name: Jun Yuh
creators.desc: Built 8M followers on his own becoming. Frameworks for digging a real story out of your own life and arcing it from problem to payoff, plus the system to post it every week.

core.name: Storytelling core
core.desc: Every story that works does four things: it makes the viewer predict, it makes them feel, it earns their trust, and it leaves one idea that sticks. The ten principles hang from this ball, and every technique links back here.

principles.name: Prediction & curiosity
principles.desc: The viewer's brain is predicting, not just watching. Open a gap they want closed, and give just enough context for them to guess.

principles.name: Stakes & conflict
principles.desc: Something must be at risk for someone the viewer roots for. No conflict, no story.

principles.name: The hook
principles.desc: The first seconds break autopilot scrolling and answer two questions: what is this about, and what do I get?

principles.name: Trust in seconds
principles.desc: Right after the hook the viewer checks: was I baited, and is this person worth hearing? Earn belief early.

principles.name: Loops & momentum
principles.desc: Keep opening new questions as you close old ones, so there's always a reason to stay for the next line.

principles.name: Specifics & feeling
principles.desc: Real details and real emotions make the brain live the story instead of just hearing it.

principles.name: One named idea
principles.desc: A story earns its time by leaving one idea the viewer can use and repeat.

principles.name: Belief & enemy
principles.desc: A story with a point of view travels. A belief people can agree or argue with is what makes them care.

principles.name: Delivery & voice
principles.desc: The same story lands or dies on how it's told: to one person, in your own voice, with rhythm.

principles.name: World & following
principles.desc: One story earns a view. Many stories inside one world earn a follower.

principles.name: Aryan: raw facts
principles.desc: Everything Aryan has said about himself, kept in his own words and sourced. Each fact is strung to the storytelling balls it relates to, so material and method can be mixed.

principles.name: Practice log
principles.desc: What Aryan has been taught, tried, answered and tested. The loop writes here after every lesson, so the network learns how he learns.

nodes.name: Dopamine = prediction
nodes.desc: Dopamine fires while we guess, not when we win. A slot machine hooks people; a vending machine doesn't.

nodes.name: Context + conflict = curiosity
nodes.desc: Tension makes people lean in. Give the setting, then the problem.

nodes.name: 4 inputs of curiosity
nodes.desc: A knowledge gap, belief the gap will be filled, novelty, and relevance. You control the inputs, not curiosity itself.

nodes.name: 5 reveal outcomes
nodes.desc: Worse than expected, as expected or confusing loses viewers. Better than expected or unexpected-but-intriguing keeps them.

nodes.name: Specifics to predict with
nodes.desc: 'Something crazy happened' gives the brain nothing. Specifics let viewers guess, and guessing is the hook.

nodes.name: Illusion of novelty
nodes.desc: A new angle on an old thing, set against a belief they already hold, tied to an outcome they want.

nodes.name: The 4 N's filter
nodes.desc: Is the idea net new, non-obvious, nuanced and observable? If not, sharpen it before you tell it.

nodes.name: Story lenses
nodes.desc: Everyone covers the obvious angle. Find yours: on Taylor Swift at the Super Bowl he covered her business impact on the NFL.

nodes.name: Flex, then subvert
nodes.desc: 'My Ferrari went up $300K… that's not even the most exciting thing today.' A gap opens mid-sentence.

nodes.name: Old things, new people
nodes.desc: Repackage fundamental truths with new framing instead of chasing brand-new ideas. Aayush taught the same six-viral-videos method as a skit in 2025 and as a talking head in 2026.
nodes.source: storytelling-playbook.md + creator research notes; sources/research/notes_aayush.md §Old reels (Dec 2024 to Sep 2025), DMA_-JqpfxX

nodes.name: Stakes
nodes.desc: A character to root for, something at risk, and urgency. It doesn't need to be life or death, just personally relevant. Adley: "Stakes determine why people care."

nodes.name: The dance: but / therefore
nodes.desc: Between beats put 'but' or 'therefore', never 'and then' (the South Park rule).

nodes.name: Call out the consequence
nodes.desc: 'Tired of wearing a hat all the time?' beats 'Tired of being bald?' Name what the pain costs them.

nodes.name: Negative frames
nodes.desc: Loss aversion: avoiding pain motivates about twice as much. 'This is killing your growth.'

nodes.name: Have a villain
nodes.desc: A person, a group, an approach or a belief. Without one, nothing pushes back.

nodes.name: Something to root for
nodes.desc: Build common ground so viewers see themselves as the hero.

nodes.name: Start at 70 out of 100
nodes.desc: Skip the school story arc. Open high, spike the first conflict early, then peak and release.

nodes.name: Aggravate the pain
nodes.desc: In a story that sells: aggravate the pain, show the old method failing, then tease a named new mechanism. Jun puts the same beat first in every story, because shared struggle is the fastest common ground there is.

nodes.name: MAP: broad pain, then specific
nodes.desc: Mission, then Attack the broad pain for reach, then Pinpoint the specific pain to pull the right viewers.

nodes.name: Conflict makes them lean in
nodes.desc: No conflict, no curiosity. Put the problem on screen before the answer, or nobody waits for the answer.

nodes.name: Interrupt theory
nodes.desc: A hook triggers the involuntary 'wait, what was that?' freeze: the orienting response.

nodes.name: The 4 S's
nodes.desc: Subject (crystal clear), Stakes (the outcome), Speed (fewest words), Super clear (only one way to read it).

nodes.name: Triple hook
nodes.desc: Text, visual and spoken hooks must all point the same way. Misalignment is the most common mistake.

nodes.name: The 6 hook words
nodes.desc: Subject, action, objective, contrast, plus an optional proof word ('again') and time word ('in 90 days').

nodes.name: HEIT hook
nodes.desc: Context + a contrarian take + an open loop: 'Trial reels aren't dead, they're just misunderstood.'

nodes.name: Wrapping paper
nodes.desc: Packaging, hook and format: your only advantage before the click. Keep a library of packaging that stops you.

nodes.name: 3 hook rules
nodes.desc: Never attack the viewer. Speak to what they want, not what they should do. Make the payoff obvious with a number, time or outcome.

nodes.name: 1 idea, 7 hooks
nodes.desc: Negative spin, positive spin, a question, an experience, a call-out, 'here's how', social proof. In mid-2025 it was three formats: shock value, demonstration, challenge.
nodes.source: storytelling-playbook.md + creator research notes; sources/research/notes_aayush.md §Old reels (Dec 2024 to Sep 2025), DK7nVlEAQbH

nodes.name: Visual hooks & props
nodes.desc: Move the camera, move yourself, hold a prop. Show while you tell; props beat heavy editing.

nodes.name: Name the plot
nodes.desc: The first line says what the story is about. Never 'wait till you see this'.

nodes.name: Lock-in zone
nodes.desc: The 1-3 lines after the hook take curiosity from 1 to 10 while viewers run a quick trust check.

nodes.name: 6 lock-in moves
nodes.desc: Tease the proof, tease the transformation, rapid contrast, frame the magic box, handle the objection, double down.

nodes.name: Bullseye proof
nodes.desc: Proof from someone just like the viewer beats 'lots of people', which beats a study.

nodes.name: Contextual credibility
nodes.desc: Proof that fits this exact topic, not your generic bio.

nodes.name: 4 C's intro
nodes.desc: Call-out, credibility, compass (the roadmap), and a core learning in the first ~60 seconds.

nodes.name: Triple P
nodes.desc: Promise what they'll learn, prove you're qualified, show the plan.

nodes.name: Proof on screen
nodes.desc: View-count badges, client profiles, dashboards: proof the eye sees before the ear processes it.

nodes.name: Expert or student
nodes.desc: Posing as an expert while you're a student burns trust. An honest learning journey earns it. Jun splits it into Expert POV (proven systems) and Journey POV ("I posted for six months and lost 100 followers, here's what NOT to do").

nodes.name: Story loops
nodes.desc: Context opens a loop, a reveal closes it, and the next opens. A 45-60 second short holds 3-4 loops. Adley calls it the itch you create and refuse to scratch.

nodes.name: Addiction loop
nodes.desc: Stakes, then big question, then head fake, then rehook. The last three repeat to the end.

nodes.name: Head fake
nodes.desc: Break their prediction with an answer that surprises but makes sense in hindsight. Plant the clues first.

nodes.name: Rehook
nodes.desc: Close one loop and open the next in one breath: 'which would have been great, except…'

nodes.name: Loop openers
nodes.desc: Reset the attention hourglass: 'But that's not even the most interesting part.'

nodes.name: Contrast words
nodes.desc: But, actually, instead, turns out, except, yet: the engine under every story lock.

nodes.name: Asymmetric pacing
nodes.desc: Make the first point the shortest. Fast early progress feels like momentum.

nodes.name: Progressive density
nodes.desc: Open with a broad problem everyone feels, then get more tactical toward the end.

nodes.name: Numbered bodies
nodes.desc: Steps, phases, months, acronyms. A number tells viewers where they are and how much is left.

nodes.name: Promise, progress, payoff
nodes.desc: Promise the payoff early, show progress toward it, then pay it off in full. Never promise five lessons and hide them; bait breaks trust for good.

nodes.name: Only essential context
nodes.desc: Where were you, when was it, what were you doing? Then straight to the conflict.

nodes.name: Thoughts & emotions
nodes.desc: Ask 'what was I thinking?' and 'what was I feeling?' Facts alone sound robotic.

nodes.name: Order the W's
nodes.desc: Lead with what and why, then who and how, then when and where as colour.

nodes.name: Paint the picture
nodes.desc: Use visuals. Show while you tell.

nodes.name: Thought narration
nodes.desc: Say what the viewer is thinking right now: 'You're probably thinking this can't work for you.'

nodes.name: Admission lines
nodes.desc: Name your own struggles out loud. It's part of being a likable expert.

nodes.name: Losses beat wins
nodes.desc: Admitting a miss builds more trust than showing a win.

nodes.name: Share weaknesses
nodes.desc: Flaws you can change, limits you adapt to, costs your choices forced on you. Real, never contrived.

nodes.name: Lived experience
nodes.desc: Educational content drawn from what you've actually been through beats an AI-written script. Jun's whole brand is this: his biggest videos are all the same becoming story.

nodes.name: Rhythm
nodes.desc: Vary sentence length. One sentence per line; the script's right edge should look jagged.

nodes.name: Teach one thing
nodes.desc: One simple idea they can apply today, not a 7-step list.

nodes.name: Point, Explain, Illustrate, Lesson
nodes.desc: Each section makes a point, explains it, illustrates it, and lands a lesson.

nodes.name: Illustrate with analogy
nodes.desc: Link the unknown to the known: content without a plan is a puzzle without the picture on the box.

nodes.name: Name your concepts
nodes.desc: Names that pass the 3 R's: easy to remember, repeat and reference. Jun names everything he teaches (L.I.F.E., the 3Ps, the wheel, 3-1-2-1); Adley names her methods too (the combo method, the Missy Elliott method).

nodes.name: Term branding
nodes.desc: The labeling effect: 'improve your offer' becomes Hormozi's 'value equation'.

nodes.name: Atomic shareability
nodes.desc: Shrink the idea to one sentence. Say it twice: once to a colleague, once as a metaphor for a child.

nodes.name: The last dab
nodes.desc: Write the last line first. Make it worth repeating; in a short it loops back to the hook. Aayush ends mid-line ('Till then…') so his last words run straight into his first.
nodes.source: storytelling-playbook.md + creator research notes; sources/research/notes_aayush.md §Old reels (Dec 2024 to Sep 2025), DOxIdPWkR9B

nodes.name: Shared language
nodes.desc: Coin phrases and repeat them for years until the audience says them back.

nodes.name: Redefine terms
nodes.desc: Give vague industry words an operational definition. Own the definition, own the conversation.

nodes.name: Named systems
nodes.desc: MAP, Pull / Prove / Connect, ONYX: a named method makes advice feel like a tool.

nodes.name: Contrarian belief
nodes.desc: The 80% lever: something you genuinely believe against the dominant view. Contrarian, not controversial.

nodes.name: Two-column exercise
nodes.desc: Left: what your space says that you disagree with. Right: your view. Keep the takes you'd defend for years.

nodes.name: Common enemy
nodes.desc: Your belief reframed as what stands between the viewer and their goal. A belief or approach, never a person.

nodes.name: One hill to die on
nodes.desc: If everyone agrees with you, you're probably not saying anything.

nodes.name: Contrarian take vault
nodes.desc: Whenever you disagree with something you watch, write down your alternative view.

nodes.name: Embedded truths
nodes.desc: Speak as if it's already true: 'When you try this', not 'If you try this'.

nodes.name: Protect the illusion
nodes.desc: Don't hedge. Deliver like a whisperer sharing a secret, not a town crier.

nodes.name: Self-articulation
nodes.desc: Say what viewers feel but can't put into words.

nodes.name: Contrarian hooks in action
nodes.desc: 'The biggest scam in content is crazy editing.' 'Never post raw talking heads.' 'I will die on this hill.'

nodes.name: Talk to one friend
nodes.desc: Talk with people, not at them. Write and film for one close friend.

nodes.name: Say 'you', end low, pause
nodes.desc: 'You', not 'you guys'. Downward inflection, no upspeak. Let the pauses breathe.

nodes.name: Be yourself, minus the friction
nodes.desc: Delivery isn't performing; it's removing what stops you being you. Calm people stay calm.

nodes.name: Likable expert
nodes.desc: Authority + affinity: believe your words, be happy to be there, be proof-heavy, admit struggles.

nodes.name: Camera anxiety kit
nodes.desc: Shake out for 30 seconds, do throwaway takes, tape a friend's photo by the lens, record line by line.

nodes.name: Copy speech
nodes.desc: Read a top creator's transcript aloud in sync with their video to absorb rhythm and pauses.

nodes.name: Hands & starts
nodes.desc: Hold something to kill awkward hands. Say 'Okay, so' before the hook, then cut it, so you start mid-thought.

nodes.name: Spoken, not written
nodes.desc: Read the script aloud and fix lines that sound written. Aim for a grade 5-7 reading level; cut for value per second.

nodes.name: Script, then outline
nodes.desc: Script word for word while learning; move to outlines once comfortable. Tangents feel real.

nodes.name: Reps beat talent
nodes.desc: Get on more stages and review your own game tape. Volume negates luck. Aayush: your first 30 videos will suck, push through anyway. Adley: "This isn't a time thing. It's definitely a reps thing."
nodes.source: storytelling-playbook.md + creator research notes; sources/research/notes_aayush.md (DePGd1Nsugv, FEfeRjrHHmc)

nodes.name: Dopamine ladder
nodes.desc: Stimulation, captivation, anticipation, validation, then affection and revelation: they like you and expect more.

nodes.name: World building
nodes.desc: Name concepts, redefine terms, share weaknesses, characters and settings, interest stacking, lore, a common enemy.

nodes.name: Characters & settings
nodes.desc: A recurring cast and recurring places. Aayush calls it building the 'characters' people recognise you by.

nodes.name: Interest stacking
nodes.desc: Your non-niche interests move viewers from acquaintance to friend to best friend.

nodes.name: Lore & legends
nodes.desc: Success and failure stories, each paired with a lesson, kept in a credibility bank.

nodes.name: Content people share to label themselves
nodes.desc: People share what says something about them. Make content they want to be seen sharing.

nodes.name: Character diamond
nodes.desc: North star, kryptonite, non-negotiables, weird interests. People follow characters.

nodes.name: Series & 'start here'
nodes.desc: Episodes that end with 'follow for part 2', and a pinned intro that tells newcomers who you are.

nodes.name: Pull / Prove / Connect
nodes.desc: Pull gets you found, Prove earns trust, Connect (your story) makes them choose you.

nodes.name: Power of suggestion
nodes.desc: Signal, belief, action: let viewers reach the conclusion themselves; people trust what they conclude.

nodes.name: Brand mission and conditions
nodes.desc: Personal brand around himself, not his company. Brand-new account from 0 followers and 0 following. He will not use his current account or network. 90 days on camera. Starts after exams end on 4 Nov 2026.

nodes.name: Goal: master storytelling first
nodes.desc: Main goal is to become an excellent storyteller. Before choosing content he wants to understand how storytelling works. Current phase: learn the frameworks, not what to post.

nodes.name: Belief: discipline and boredom
nodes.desc: Consistency, discipline, honour and character can achieve anything. Learn fast and get "addicted to the boredom of the slow process of life".

nodes.name: Belief line (picked)
nodes.desc: "Discipline without direction is just a better 9-to-5." The gym taught discipline; the internship showed him it needs direction.

nodes.name: Origin: gym, internship, no 9-to-5
nodes.desc: The gym taught consistency. Seniors repeating the same routine for years and the commute made him say "not this life". He wants to be free and build his own legacy.

nodes.name: Mission: change his bloodline
nodes.desc: "I have to change my bloodline." Born middle class; will die rich and make his parents proud. Legacy = a portfolio of companies, family financially free, his name as a brand.

nodes.name: Story: the doubt night
nodes.desc: Lowest moment of the past year: doubting the whole path, alone late at night with zero results. One voice says keep going; he calls one or two people to cross-check; he shows up again.

nodes.name: Story: the cold-calling saga
nodes.desc: 300-350 calls to interior designers, all "no". Asked 2-3 friends and a 25-year sales mentor, researched with Claude, switched to manufacturers, stopped at 100 calls with under 10 interested. Friends said cold calling is weak in India, so he went store to store in Hiranandani.

nodes.name: Story: the first store
nodes.desc: Nervous before the first meeting; held one thought: the mind takes the path of least resistance, so do the opposite. Dropped the script and pitched. The first 10 conversations were just understanding. Open: is he comfortable with shop owners now? Added 22-23 Oct: the real fault was a frame switch. He walked in as a student asking for a student interview, then tried to close as a founder, which is why the conversation turned awkward and why he wondered whether the owner was too protective to let a student help. His thought at the time: the student part went fine, the founder part he lost. Body tells he can now name: his palms go wet once pricing starts; the owner took a phone call mid-pitch and came back with "okay, so bottom line, you're trying to tell me this", compressing the whole pitch into one line; and the owner held eye contact for five or six seconds at a time before looking away.

nodes.name: Proof inventory
nodes.desc: 300+ cold calls, automations and AI agents built, three paying clients (see x073; names hidden is fine). OK to show: calls, rejections, his screen while building, struggles. Not chosen: revenue numbers, home and family.

nodes.name: Audience: undecided, three candidates
nodes.desc: Students 17-24, small business owners, founders ahead of him. He can help a scared would-be founder, a 12th-grader at a crossroads, a shop owner drowning in manual work. Wants viewers to feel "I can do this too". Update 4 Nov: for the next 90 days he chose owners of existing businesses (see x076).

nodes.name: Delivery setup
nodes.desc: Hinglish, English or Hindi, open to all. Phone only (OnePlus Nord CE 3 Lite). 3-5 hours a week. Always wears glasses. Tone: occasional swearing, raw. Has filmed a few times.

nodes.name: Interests and content taste
nodes.desc: Could talk 2 hours on how AI changes work, building a business at 19, discipline. Could make 10 videos on gym and body, or middle-class Indian life. Watches Hormozi-style breakdowns, founder journeys, AI tool breakdowns. Does not want it to be only yapping.

nodes.name: How he wants Claude to work
nodes.desc: Ask psychological and situational questions over time and double down on patterns. Use skills by default. Give one clear direction. Concise, blunt, pure English.

nodes.name: Home: supportive, studies first
nodes.desc: Family says okay but studies must not be compromised; sometimes "stop this, get a good job". They know bits and pieces of what he does.

nodes.name: Lesson map: six layers (all taught)
nodes.desc: The teaching path has six layers: brain (prediction), atom (the loop), engine (the addiction loop), door (the hook), feeling (thoughts and emotions), meaning (the named idea). All six taught by 23 Oct 2026. Next is the capstone: three full scripts. Running test score 11/24.

nodes.name: Lesson 1 result: the brain predicts (1.5/3)
nodes.desc: Answered. He got that B makes the brain guess, and that the guessing itself is where the pull comes from. Missed which input B adds: said relevance when the answer is the knowledge gap. Then wrote a hook of his own with the same fault he had just been shown, using 'this' as the mystery. Retest passed on the second attempt. The lesson behind the lesson: the skill is spotting an input that is present but weak, not just present or absent.

nodes.name: Rule: the network is a loop
nodes.desc: Aryan's rule: every new fact, edit or deletion in this project goes into the network, so it becomes a competitive edge that improves over time.

nodes.name: Rule: Code keeps the network, chat teaches
nodes.desc: Aryan, 2026-10-16: Claude Code sessions do not teach. Their job is to keep the network easy to reach, string everything together and run tests (validation, relink and pattern passes, mix tests). Lessons happen in the claude.ai Personal Brand chat.

nodes.name: Argue it out: two-character skit
nodes.desc: Play both sides. One character has the problem, the other has the fix, so the conflict is built into the format and a plain tutorial becomes a scene.

nodes.name: Demonstrate it inside the reel
nodes.desc: Use the technique while you teach it, then point it out: 'I bet you didn't notice I used both.' The viewer gets the lesson and the proof in the same seconds.
nodes.source: sources/research/notes_aayush.md §Old reels (Dec 2024 to Sep 2025), DK7nVlEAQbH; notes_aayush.md O-GXIw8YWvY, tGYh79FnOq8

nodes.name: Name it so they can say it back
nodes.desc: All four creators turn advice into a named thing: Kallaway's term branding, Caleb's named concepts, Sam's shared language, Aayush's named systems. A name makes an idea easy to remember, repeat and credit to you.
nodes.source: pattern pass 2026-10-16 over p7e, p7d, p7h, p7j

nodes.name: Take a side you'd defend
nodes.desc: All four push a genuine opposing view: Caleb's contrarian belief, Sam's one hill to die on, Kallaway's take vault, Aayush's die-on-this-hill hooks. Aim it at a belief, not a person, and keep only sides you'd still hold in a year.
nodes.source: pattern pass 2026-10-16 over p8a, p8d, p8e, p8i, p8c

nodes.name: Prove it before they doubt it
nodes.desc: All four put proof right after the hook: Kallaway's bullseye proof, Caleb's contextual credibility, Sam's Triple P, Aayush's proof on screen. The proof must fit this claim and this viewer, and land before the trust check ends.
nodes.source: pattern pass 2026-10-16 over p4c, p4d, p4f, p4g

nodes.name: Admit the miss
nodes.desc: Kallaway's admission lines, Sam's losses beat wins and Caleb's shared weaknesses agree: a real flaw or failure, said plainly, buys more trust than another win.
nodes.source: pattern pass 2026-10-16 over p6f, p6g, p6h

nodes.name: People follow characters
nodes.desc: Caleb's characters and settings, Aayush's 'build your characters' and Sam's character diamond agree: viewers follow a recognisable person with recurring places, objects, quirks and limits, not a topic.

nodes.name: Sync: chat writes to GitHub, Code watches
nodes.desc: Aryan, 2026-10-16: the Personal Brand chat has a project instruction to write every new thing to GitHub, either into a markdown file or as direct changes. No Google Doc. The Claude Code session checks the repo twice a day (about 13:56 and 22:56 IST) and ingests whatever landed.

nodes.name: Lesson 2 result: loops and reveals (2/3)
nodes.desc: Taught story loops, the 5 reveal outcomes, but/therefore and essential context. Scored 2/3. Got 'as expected' and 'unexpected but confusing' right; called an unexpected-but-intriguing reveal 'worse than expected', so he read a failed outcome as a dead loop when a new question had actually opened. Half right on but/therefore: used 'but' correctly for a new problem, then used it again for a consequence that needed 'so'. Full marks on cutting context down to where, when and what.

nodes.name: Lesson 3 result: the engine (3/3, found extra)
nodes.desc: Taught the addiction loop: stakes, big question, head fake, rehook. Full marks, and he spotted flaws that were not planted. On his own he worked out the dependency chain: no stakes means nobody cares, so nobody predicts, so there is nothing to fake and nothing to rehook. His best round of the course. Weak spot: his own written answers kept using vague nouns ('inappropriate results') while he was busy catching the same fault in the examples.

nodes.name: Lesson 4 result: the hook (needed a replay)
nodes.desc: Taught interrupt theory, the 4 S's, the 6 hook words and the triple hook. He said plainly he did not understand the 6 hook words as first explained; the labels were too abstract. Re-explained with a plain worked example and he then found all six slots, but shifted three of them: gave 'land client' as subject, '3 client' as action, 'in 30 days 3 client' as objective. He can see the parts; he cannot yet name which part is which.

nodes.name: Lesson 5 result: feeling (breakthrough after 5 misses)
nodes.desc: Taught thoughts and emotions over labels, and that losses build more trust than wins. He missed the body-detail task five times running, each time answering with an urge or a tactic instead ('wanted to end it fast', 'spitting facts'). Concept, template and worked examples all failed. What worked was a forced-choice list of concrete body signals to pick from, which produced three usable details in one reply. Teaching note: when an abstract instruction fails twice, switch to recognition before asking him to produce.

nodes.name: Lesson 6 result: meaning (0.5/6, worst round)
nodes.desc: Taught name it, last line first, one sentence, enemy and badge. Scored 0.5/6. Classification of the five mechanisms: 0/3. His name for a given idea ('demand fulfilment') was abstract jargon that fails the 3 R's. On contrarian versus controversial he picked the right line but justified it by why it would work, which is the exact trap. Part of this is a teaching error: a five-item taxonomy handed over at midnight and then tested on classification.

nodes.name: Leak: he answers with the result, not the thing
nodes.desc: His single most repeated habit, across three lessons and two sessions, so not fatigue. Asked for a body detail he gave the urge it produced. Asked to name an idea he gave the outcome it leads to. Asked for an enemy he gave the consequence of the enemy. Every time the question asked for something concrete and he reached one step past it to what it causes. Fix in use: before sending an answer, ask whether a person could see, hear or touch it, or whether it is only what that thing causes.

nodes.name: Leak: vague gaps in his own writing
nodes.desc: He reliably catches a vague curiosity gap in someone else's line and then writes one himself in the next breath: 'this', 'inappropriate results', 'diamond move', 'pitch rate increased', '15 quality info'. He also tends to name the mystery and explain it one clause later, which closes the gap before it can pull. The test to run on his own lines: could a stranger guess what comes next.

nodes.name: Skill profile: recognise > produce > classify
nodes.desc: Three clear tiers from six lessons. Recognising a flaw in someone else's line is his strength, including flaws not planted. Producing the thing himself usually fails on the first attempt and lands on the second. Naming which category or mechanism something belongs to is his weakest by a distance. He has intuition without taxonomy: he feels that a line is wrong before he can say which rule it breaks. Drill the naming, not the spotting.

nodes.name: Absorption: comprehension breaks at minute 62
nodes.desc: From message timestamps across two separate sessions. Session of 20 Oct began 00:49; at minute 62 he said he did not understand. Session of 22-23 Oct began 23:21; at minute 64 he scored 0.5/6, his worst round. Two sessions two days apart, and the wall lands within two minutes of the same place. Everything before minute 50 was decent in both. Also: 16 of 18 timestamped messages fall between 23:00 and 02:30, and he has never run a lesson in daylight, so his measured capacity is his floor, not his range. Rule set: hard stop at 45 minutes.

nodes.name: Absorption: structures stick, flat lists do not
nodes.desc: Read-once retention of concepts is good and his worry about forgetting is not supported. He has never once asked for a concept from an earlier session to be re-explained, and after a 47-hour gap he opened with full marks. What held: but/therefore and the 5 reveal outcomes, both built as contrasts. What did not: the 4 curiosity inputs (he named relevance as weakest twice when it was his strongest) and the 5 meaning mechanisms (0/3). He remembers structures and sequences, not inventories of four or five parallel items. Teach in pairs and contrasts; never test five-way classification.

nodes.name: Rule: more examples, fewer questions about him
nodes.desc: Aryan, 22 Oct: his sole purpose in this phase is to get good at storytelling, so lessons should carry more examples and only around one question tied to his own life. Agreed format per lesson: concept, four real examples broken down beat by beat, two counter-examples showing why the weak version dies, drills on other people's material, then one rep on his own, banked and moved past. Roughly 70 per cent other people's work. Separate error owned: one answer was chased across five turns instead of giving it, showing a worked example and re-testing two lessons later.

nodes.name: Emotion plus a gap
nodes.desc: Her hook rule, stated flat: "Every hook must elicit an emotional response and open up a gap in curiosity." One without the other fails. A gap with no feeling is trivia; a feeling with no gap has nothing left to watch for.

nodes.name: The combo method
nodes.desc: Pair two things that do not normally go together, so the brain cannot place what it is seeing. Her example: a rack of ribs cooking on a car engine.

nodes.name: 90% through six seconds
nodes.desc: Her retention target for the opening: 90% still watching at six seconds, 82% still good, and about 75% through the first twelve seconds as the sign a video can travel. "The first three seconds matter more than the next 30 ever will."

nodes.name: The Missy Elliott method
nodes.desc: Put it down, flip it and reverse it: design the video backwards from its opening three seconds. Open on an intriguing scene, never on your end goal, and pitch the opening shot rather than the payoff.

nodes.name: Hold the payoff
nodes.desc: Give value the whole way through but resolve the curiosity gap only in the last 3-10 seconds. "There is a subconscious itch there that I created that I am not going to scratch." Leaving it unresolved on purpose is how you force a part two.

nodes.name: Four stakes levers
nodes.desc: Four cheap ways to raise what is at risk. Location: get out of the expected setting. Props: raise the value of the thing that could break. Wardrobe: signal character with no explanation. Casting: pick people whose presence changes the weight, like a child or a couple in their seventies.

nodes.name: Engineer the comment section
nodes.desc: Decide what you want people to comment before you film, then build the triggers in: Easter eggs, a relatable moment, debate bait, odd wardrobe, a deliberate gap that lets viewers show their expertise.

nodes.name: Split test before you post
nodes.desc: Make 3-4 versions of the same video with different hooks, opening shots, lengths and captions. Load 5-12 onto trial reels, let them run 24-72 hours, then publish the winner to the feed. Paid version: $5-6 a variant, about 1,000 views to read a curve.

nodes.name: Cut at the 40% drop
nodes.desc: Read the retention curve and find where it falls off a cliff. A drop of 40% or more names the beat to rewrite. Writing version: check the script every three seconds and ask whether they would keep watching, and why anyone cares.

nodes.name: One emotional tone
nodes.desc: Pick the emotion before you write: learning, humour, fear or trust. Then hold it. Switching tone mid-video confuses people and they leave. Music and text overlays set that tone, so the same footage reads differently under suspenseful music.

nodes.name: Contextual vs cultural relevance
nodes.desc: Contextual relevance is being known for a service inside your niche. Cultural relevance is broad shareable appeal. Cultural makes you contextually relevant by default; the reverse is not true.

nodes.name: Virality is subjective
nodes.desc: The bar is set by your own channel, not by the internet. Her company counts 5 million views as viral; a channel that normally does 300-400 views can honestly call 40,000 viral.

nodes.name: Most of it is top of funnel
nodes.desc: Aim for 60% or more of your posts to be awareness content built for people who do not know you, because shares are what the algorithm weights and what finds lookalike audiences.

nodes.name: L.I.F.E. story buckets
nodes.desc: Every personal story fits at least one of four buckets: Love, Identity, Fitness, Earnings. Stuck for a post? Pick a letter first, then pick the story. Better still when two buckets overlap.

nodes.name: Ask why three times
nodes.desc: After you pick the story, ask why three times. The first answer is surface. The second is more honest. The third is where you are actually vulnerable, and that is the one worth telling.

nodes.name: The storytelling wheel: safe, real, raw
nodes.desc: Safe is a surface description of what happened. Raw is the why and the deeper emotion underneath it. His line: the safe story gets you attention, the raw one gets people to relate to you. Bad creators stay on the surface, average creators jump around, the best stay in the raw.

nodes.name: The 3P arc: problem, pursuit, payoff
nodes.desc: His story arc. Open on the problem, show the pursuit, land the payoff. Then package the same three beats into a format you can repeat.

nodes.name: Lead with the problem, not your success
nodes.desc: "Most creators make the mistake of starting their videos with personal successes to earn the viewer's trust, however it's actually turning viewers away." The fancy car and the house push people out. His objection is to status as the opener, not to proof itself: prove you understand their problem, not that you have escaped it.

nodes.name: Silent film format
nodes.desc: No talking at all. On-screen text, B-roll and music. Start with pain, because you do not need footage from the real moment, only words for the feeling. Skip trending sounds and pick audio with rising action. The music drop is the payoff moment.

nodes.name: No one else is a prop
nodes.desc: Never tell someone else's story. None of his storytelling videos speak badly about his mother, his father or an ex, and he keeps his girlfriend's name private. Every story stays on his own maturation, so nobody can accuse him of monetising someone else's pain.

nodes.name: Land on the transformation
nodes.desc: Never park on the pain. The story has to resolve into "here is who I became because of it". That resolution is the difference between useful and merely sad, and it is what stops a feed becoming a highlight reel of curated wounds.

nodes.name: Creator Vision: what, who, why
nodes.desc: One page, three branches. What: your message and the pillars under it. Who: the person you make it for. Why: your own stories. He calls a blank Why branch the whole gap between 100K followers and a million, and says "what do I post today?" is a symptom of it. Takes about 30 minutes on paper.

nodes.name: Become the niche
nodes.desc: The advice says pick a micro-topic and stay in it. His objection: you evolve, your interests shift, your story expands, and the niche boxes you in. Build the brand on your story, values and message instead, create around your pillars, and the audience grows with you.

Seven posts a week, each with a job. Three attract (storytelling, usually struggle) to bring new people. One nurture: real life, no lesson, no arc, which is the release valve that stops the storytelling calcifying. Two position (insight, systems) for authority. One convert, a clear path to work with you.

nodes.name: The younger you
nodes.desc: When you do not know what to make, make it for the version of yourself from two or three years ago. You already know exactly what he needed to hear and what he would have clicked on.

nodes.name: Study format, not substance
nodes.desc: Learn from creators in any industry by copying the format, never the story. His checklist for taking a format apart: hook, visuals and editing, cadence, audio, story arc, CTA. Then plan by date, your own ideas, and the formats you have studied.

nodes.name: Complexity kills consistency
nodes.desc: Equipment is an excuse; the repeatable system is the asset. He grew the first three million followers on a shattered iPhone 12. The system: three batch phases (script, film, edit) plus a scene library of 50+ labelled B-roll folders, so nobody has to film to post.

nodes.name: Valuable, not viral
nodes.desc: Separate the content that gets attention from the content that earns trust, and build the product from what the audience actually asks for. He surveyed his audience twice a week for three months before launching one. Old posts keep selling, so every post needs a job.

nodes.name: Retention is the honest vote
nodes.desc: Likes and comments can be bought or bantered into existence. Staying cannot. She optimises for retention above everything because it is the one signal that says the viewer thought the next second was worth it, and it is the signal the algorithm trusts too.

nodes.name: Three hook archetypes
nodes.desc: The three openings that recur across his reels: a contrarian declaration that challenges an industry norm, a vulnerable confession of sudden crisis, and a visual misdirection that sets a false premise before the twist.

nodes.name: Offer today: end-to-end systems, retainer
nodes.desc: What he sells now: end-to-end systems for businesses that replace a salaried role. His claim: about 5x output on that task. Build takes 7-10 days, then a monthly maintenance or upgrade fee that he puts of ₹10,000 for software (corrected 4 Nov, see x074; earlier he said 500 to 10000). Own words for the buyer: businesses that need efficiency optimisation through proper systems and a bigger audience. The 5x claim has no software client behind it; his three paying clients are marketing work (see x073).

nodes.name: Runway and commitment
nodes.desc: Needs cash within about 3 months. Will not quit the personal brand: he has "nowhere else to go". Would reconsider direction only after 6-7 months of consistent posting with bare-minimum results. No day-30/60/90 metric set yet.

nodes.name: Constraint: age and stage when charging for guidance
nodes.desc: Says his age and stage worry him a lot when charging for advice and it would hold him back. Wants proven outcomes before he charges for guidance. Does not yet know who the viewer is (audience still open, x011). Energy and content taste lean to talking, guiding and teaching frameworks; exit preference is recurring membership income.

nodes.name: Direction exam: community vs clients
nodes.desc: 4 Nov: took a 10 MCQ + 3 short-answer exam to choose between a paid community (guidance sessions for early founders) and clients from content. MCQ lean as first submitted: 4 community, 5 clients. Corrected same evening: Q1 proof is actually three client jobs; Q4 energised by both talking and building; Q5 right option but wants early founders to feel DM-reachable; Q8 can show work from three clients. Corrected lean: 1 community, 7 clients, 1 neutral (my recount). Preference answers (energy, exit, teaching) lean community; evidence answers (cash in 3 months, proof, age worry, DM sales) lean clients. Weak spots found: B2 gave categories, not a count of people who would pay in 30 days; offer price range is 20x wide; kill criteria are time-based, not metric-based; Q1 vs Q5 conflict resolved: he has three clients but no stated outcomes. New weak spots: nothing yet shows results, spa delivery is short (140 of 250 messages, reviews dropped), software prices have no software client behind them. Verdict given in chat: clients first, community later built on client proof. Not yet decided by Aryan.

nodes.name: Clients so far: three, all small
nodes.desc: Three paying clients, ₹7,500 collected in total (private, not for camera). (1) Tissue paper manufacturer, a college friend: 4 reels for ₹4,500. (2) Spa: ₹5,000 deal, ₹2,000 paid so far; owes 4 reels and 4 posts plus a revival campaign: 140 of about 250 promised messages sent. Google Maps reviews were promised but cannot be automated or bought, so he will drop them and send 100 extra messages as compensation. (3) Cycle retail shop: 2 posts and 3 reels for ₹1,000, a lead from an earlier "we can work for any amount" conversation. No results (replies, bookings, sales) stated for any of the three yet. No software or system client yet. Update 4 Nov: the tissue paper reels and the cycle shop posts have not been posted by the clients yet, so they carry no public proof. The only measurable thing so far is the spa revival campaign: how many people viewed the messages and how many replies came in (numbers not given yet). Software: three builds made, none paid (see x078).

nodes.name: Price ladder (INR)
nodes.desc: Software: ₹10,000 to ₹50,000, possibly ₹1 lakh, with a ₹10,000 monthly retainer. Marketing: post ₹500, reel ₹1,000; revival campaign sending 1,000 to 2,000 messages for ₹5,000 to ₹10,000; websites ₹10,000 to ₹50,000; end-to-end systems ₹20,000 to ₹2 lakh. This replaces the earlier "500 to 10000" monthly maintenance range in x069.

nodes.name: Account audience and DM stance
nodes.desc: Wants the account to speak to owners and founders who run a current business. Then to translate it for early founders: a realistic, raw view of what you actually get and what to expect, against the "start and figure it out" mindset. Also wants to reach ambitious people who might work with him, become clients, or want guidance. Wants early-stage people to feel they can just DM him, with no gatekeeping.

nodes.name: 90-day buyer and lead offer
nodes.desc: Decision on 4 Nov: for the next 90 days the one buyer is owners of existing businesses. They get software systems and marketing. The lead offer is the revival campaign (messaging past customers), which he says can also carry reels, posts, websites and branding correction. Single offer is not yet fixed: he describes the revival campaign as one of the lead-generating offers, bundled with other work.

nodes.name: Site check: atomz.online vs chosen buyer
nodes.desc: Claude fetched atomz.online on 4 Nov at his suggestion. It lists four service areas (content strategy, brand growth, monetization, operations) aimed at creators and founders, with no pricing, no client names, no results and no case studies. It does not mention revival campaigns, local businesses or his three real clients. Mismatch: his chosen 90-day buyer is owners of existing businesses. Observation by Claude, not a statement by Aryan.

nodes.name: Software builds: three made, none converted
nodes.desc: Corrects the earlier note that he had pitched software once. He has built software for three businesses and none has paid. (1) A plant nursery: they had tried a booking system before and said it did not work; asked why, got no solid answer; he offered to build one, they said yes, he built it to their detailed requirements, then the owner wrote that the software is not her priority, asked to pause because of upcoming events, and Aryan said he would ping after Diwali to decide whether to move forward. This is the green-culture build. (2) A dental clinic: he built a CRM, she said she would look into it, then said she was moving in with another doctor in the same clinic and would use their software; he insisted she look at his, she kept delaying, then said she did not need it. (3) A manufacturing shop: he built a tool-entry system because they said they were losing about ₹50,000 a year on lost tools; after follow-up they said they did not want to invest. Stated on 5 Nov. Whether any deposit or written scope was agreed before building is not yet known.

nodes.name: GitHub review: what he has built
nodes.desc: Claude read his GitHub on 4 Nov (shallow reads). Built and documented: green-culture (private) booking, UPI payment matching and travel pricing for a gardening nursery, with a demo mode, tests and a race-condition stress test; kalakruti (public) automatic payment-reminder emails with a 4-step schedule, live on Vercel; CRM (private) his own cold-call and WhatsApp outreach tracker with script-funnel analytics; AtomZ- (public) the agency marketing site, aimed at creators and founders; le-mom-zart (public) a brand site for an embroidery label; sills (private) a Claude plugin for web scraping; Reverse-Engineering (public) tool setup only; Quotation-builder- is empty. Not opened: Aryan-journal, Claude-. Whether any of these was built for a paying client is not stated. Observation by Claude from the repos, not a statement by Aryan. Update 5 Nov: Aryan says green-culture was a real build for a real nursery client, not converted (see x078). The dental CRM and the manufacturing tool-entry tool were not matched to a repo; the repo named CRM is his own outreach tracker.

nodes.name: Pattern: built before the client committed
nodes.desc: Claude diagnosis on 5 Nov from his three software cases, not yet confirmed by him. In all three he built first and asked for commitment after. Warning signs that were present before the build: the nursery could not say why their earlier system failed; the dental clinic only said she would look into it and then delayed; the manufacturer named a ₹50,000-a-year loss but a loss that size is a small problem for them to pay to fix. Words were the only commitment in each case. Test to run next: whether any money or signed scope was agreed before building. Also corrects Claude's 4 Nov line that his software proof is stronger than his marketing proof: the software shows he can build, only marketing has taken money (₹7,500 across three clients).

combos.name: The belief flip
combos.oneLine: Open on a contrarian belief, prove it on screen, then flip the viewer's guess about why.
combos.howItWorks: The contrarian line breaks autopilot because it clashes with what the viewer already believes. Proof on screen settles the 'is this bait?' check in the first seconds. The head fake then makes them predict the wrong reason, so the real one lands as a surprise that still makes sense.
recipe: Hook: say the common belief, then your opposite take, in one breath (HEIT).
Proof: show something on screen that makes the take credible in under 3 seconds.
Big question: ask why the common belief fails.
Head fake: name the reason most people would guess, then reject it.
Reveal: the real reason, with one specific detail.
Last line: restate the belief as a sentence worth repeating.

test.why: It stacks one move from each creator (Caleb's belief lever, Sam's HEIT hook, Kallaway's head fake, Aayush's proof-first opening) and none of them fight each other.
test.risk: If the proof is weak, or the take is contrarian only for shock, the trust check fails and the flip feels like bait.

combos.example:
Everyone says study 8 hours before an exam. That's the worst advice going.
[On screen: two mark sheets side by side]
So why does cramming fail?
You'd guess it's tiredness. It isn't.
Your brain keeps only what it's forced to recall, and rereading forces nothing.
Study less. Recall more.

combos.name: The argued lesson
combos.oneLine: Teach a method as a two-character argument: a wrong guess, the real fix, and a last line that cuts back into the first.
combos.howItWorks: The skit gives the lesson a built-in conflict, so viewers stay to see who's right. Letting the struggling character guess the obvious fix is a head fake. Proof on screen settles the trust check, and the loop ending sends viewers back to the start.
recipe: A states the problem as a feeling.
B pushes back with the flipped belief.
A guesses the obvious fix; B rejects it (head fake).
B gives the real method, each step shown on screen.
The last line stops mid-sentence and runs into A's first line.

test.why: The parts don't fight: the skit brings conflict, the head fake brings surprise, the proof brings trust. Aayush's July 2025 skit used three of the four and ran 69 seconds.
test.risk: Skits run long and bad acting breaks them. You speak as a character, not as yourself, so it builds less personal trust than talking to camera.

combos.example:
A: Why are you smiling?
B: I finished a week of revision in one evening.
A: How? I'd need ten hours a day.
B: That's the mistake. You don't need more hours.
A: Then a better timetable?
B: No. Test yourself first, then read only what you got wrong. [on screen: the test sheet]
A: Why are you smiling?

combos.name: Aim the hook at a belief
combos.oneLine: A negative, contrarian hook works when its target is a belief the viewer holds, not the viewer.
combos.howItWorks: Negative frames pull harder than positive ones, and contrarian lines break autopilot. Aimed at the viewer, the same energy makes them defensive and the trust check fails. Aimed at a belief, it lets the viewer side with you against it.
recipe: Name a belief the viewer holds.
Attack the belief in negative terms.
Give the replacement in the same breath.
Never make 'you' the subject of the insult.

test.why: Real case: Aayush's Dec 2024 reel has two hooks. The spoken one attacks a belief ('Likes aren't going to sign you any fitness coaching clients. Relationships do.'); the caption attacks the viewer ('Makes sense why you're still broke…'). A year later his own first hook rule is 'never attack the viewer'. Strong aimed at a belief, weak aimed at a person.
test.risk: The line is thin: 'you're doing X wrong' still lands on the viewer even when X is only a habit.

combos.example:
Weak: No wonder you're still stuck.
Strong: Rereading your notes isn't learning. Testing yourself is.

combos.name: The beginner's hot take
combos.oneLine: A contrarian claim, stated as expert truth, by someone with no proof yet.
combos.howItWorks: A contrarian belief needs proof to survive the trust check. A beginner has little, so the claim reads as bait. The working version is a different move: frame the take as a test you ran, so the experiment is the proof.
recipe: State the common belief.
Say you tested the opposite, with a time frame.
Show what happened, wins and misses.
Say what you believe now, as a student, not an expert.

test.why: Two of the three balls fight. Contrarian belief asks you to sound certain; expert-or-student says a beginner who sounds like an expert burns trust; bullseye proof needs evidence a beginner doesn't have. As an expert claim it fails. Reframed as an experiment it stops being this mix.
test.risk: It tempts beginners because contrarian hooks get views, but the views come from people who will check the proof and find none.

combos.example:
Weak: Everyone's wrong about studying, and I'll prove it.
Working version: Everyone says study 8 hours. I studied 2 a day for 30 days instead. Here's what my marks did.

combos.name: The frame you walked in with
combos.oneLine: Tell a failure where the other person never changed; your own frame did, halfway through.
combos.howItWorks: Expert-or-student says pick one frame and stay honest inside it. The story works because the viewer is handed an obvious culprit (my age, the market, a bad lead) and the real cause is the narrator quietly switching frames. Stakes make the switch matter, one thought and one body detail make it felt, and the head fake is that the antagonist did nothing wrong.
recipe: Stakes: what you wanted out of the room, in one line.
Essential context only: where, when, what you were doing.
The frame you opened with, said plainly.
One thought in your own words, one thing your body did.
The other person's action, quoted if you have their words.
Head fake: name the reason the viewer is already blaming, then reject it.
Reveal: you changed frames, and that was the whole problem.
Last line: the rule you now follow, short enough to repeat.

test.why: Tested on Aryan's first-shop story and it held with no invention needed. Every beat was already in his own account: the student-interview opening, the founder pitch, his palms, the owner's phone call and his compressing line. The head fake is unusually clean because the viewer blames his age and the answer is his own frame.
test.risk: Only works when the narrator genuinely was at fault. If the other person really did behave badly, the same shape reads as false modesty. Also needs a real quote; paraphrasing the other person kills the proof.

combos.example:
I asked a shop owner for a student interview. Twenty minutes later I was pitching him.
He took a call halfway through my price. I stood there, palms going wet, thinking: the student part went fine, the founder part I just lost.
You'd guess he said no because I'm 19. He didn't.
He hung up and said, "Okay, so bottom line, you're trying to tell me this." And he was right. He'd said my whole pitch in one line.
Pick the frame you walk in with. Then stay in it.
